title: The Year of Sorrow
teaser: He buried his protector and his wife in one season. Then he walked to Ta'if, and was stoned out of it.

layers.title: The Two Who Stood Between Him and the City
layers.subtitle: What a protector and a wife had been holding up
layers.content:
Consider what Abu Talib had actually been. He was not a believer. He never said the word. But for a decade he had put the standing of his clan behind a nephew whose message he did not accept, and Quraysh had calculated around that fact every time they moved. Al-Mubarakpuri calls him a fortress that shielded the call from the tyrants and the fools. Everything Quraysh did to the Prophet ﷺ in those years, they did knowing there was a line drawn somewhere and a man willing to defend it.

And consider Khadijah bint Khuwailid. Twenty-five years of marriage. She had been the first to believe him, on the day he came down from the cave shaking. She had spent her own wealth on him. She had absorbed the private cost of a public mission — the cost nobody records, the part where a man comes home from being called a liar in the street.

He came out of the valley of Ash-Shi'b to find that his uncle had come out of it too, at around eighty years old, and had immediately been overtaken by illness and physical weakness. The blockade had broken the man who broke the blockade.

Quraysh had cancelled the pact and gone straight back to the oppression. So the arrangement in Makkah as the tenth year of prophethood opened was this: a growing hostility outside the house, and inside it two people, one old and dying, one aging, who between them were carrying the whole weight of a man's protection and a man's peace.

They were about to go within the same season.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: Two Deaths and an Open City
layers.subtitle: The word his uncle would not say
layers.content:
Abu Talib died in Rajab of the tenth year of prophethood, six months after leaving the confinement — that is the view Al-Mubarakpuri prefers. Another report places his death in Ramadan, three days before Khadijah. Reports differ over the interval, and so over whether the two deaths were separated by days or by two or three months.

Sahih al-Bukhari carries the deathbed, narrated from al-Musayyab. The Prophet ﷺ came in and found Abu Jahl and Abdullah bin Abi Umaiyah already sitting there. He said to his uncle: my uncle, say there is no true god but Allah, and I will bear testimony before Allah for you. The two men leaned in: Abu Talib, would you abandon the religion of Abdul-Muttalib? He kept asking. They kept repeating it. Abu Talib gave his final answer, held to the religion of Abdul-Muttalib, and refused to say the word. The Prophet ﷺ said: by Allah, I will keep asking pardon for you until I am forbidden to do so.

Then Khadijah went, in Ramadan of the same year. She was sixty-five. He was fifty. Of her he said: she believed in me when the people disbelieved me, and she trusted me when the people called me a liar, and she helped and comforted me with herself and her wealth when the people would not. That is preserved in Musnad Ahmad.

Makkah understood immediately what had changed. A Quraysh man intercepted him in the street and threw sand over his head. He walked home with it in his hair and his daughter washed it out, weeping. He told her: do not weep, my daughter, Allah will protect your father. And he said afterwards: Quraysh never did anything to me like what they did after the death of Abu Talib.

Abu Bakr left the city altogether, intending Abyssinia, and only turned back when Ibn ad-Daghinah met him at Birk al-Ghimad and brought him home under his own protection.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the death of Abu Talib, narrated from al-Musayyab; and Abu Bakr's departure from Makkah
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Wall of the Vineyard
layers.subtitle: Sixty kilometres for a hearing, and none given
layers.content:
In Shawwal of the tenth year of prophethood — the end of May or the beginning of June, 619 CE — he set out on foot for Ta'if, about sixty kilometres from Makkah, with Zayd bin Harithah. He was walking to another city because his own had closed.

He went first to the family of Umair, counted among the nobility there, and got abuse. Three brothers among the chiefs of Thaqif — Abd Yalil, Mas'ud and Habib, sons of Amr bin Umair — heard him out and mocked him. One said: is it true Allah sent you, when you are tearing the drapes of the Ka'bah? The second: could Allah find nobody else to entrust with His message? The third: I swear I will never speak to you — if you are the Messenger of Allah you are too great for me to address, and if you are lying about Allah I should not address you at all.

He stood and left them with one request: since this is how you behave, do not tell anyone I was here.

He stayed ten days anyway, working from one notable to the next. Nothing. Then, to hasten the departure of their unwelcome visitor, the fools and the servants of the town chased him through the narrow lanes, pelted him with stones and drove him out — two or three miles across the sandy plain to the foot of the hills. Blood ran down both his legs. Zayd, trying to shield him, was wounded in the head.

Exhausted, he turned into one of the fruit orchards and sat down against the wall of a vineyard. Fifty years old, newly widowed, newly unprotected, bleeding, and laughed out of the only other city he had.

There he raised his hands. The words are preserved through the sirah reports of Ibn Ishaq, carried by Ibn Hisham and after him by Al-Mubarakpuri; they are not in Bukhari or Muslim, and they are given here as those sources report them. «إِلَيْكَ أَشْكُو ضَعْفَ قُوَّتِي، وَقِلَّةَ حِيلَتِي، وَهَوَانِي عَلَى النَّاسِ» — 'To You I complain of the weakness of my strength, the little I can do, and my lowliness before people.' He called Allah the Most Merciful of the merciful and the Lord of the weak, and asked into whose hands He was consigning him. He said: «أَعُوذُ بِنُورِ وَجْهِكَ الَّذِي أَشْرَقَتْ لَهُ الظُّلُمَاتُ» — 'I seek refuge in the light of Your Face, by which the darknesses are lit.' And he closed it: «وَلَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِكَ».

Notice what is absent. He asks for no punishment on Ta'if. He does not ask to be taken out. He complains of his own weakness.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam — citing Ibn Hisham

layers.title: What Answered Him on the Road
layers.subtitle: A tray of grapes, an offer refused, and a hearing given
layers.content:
The first answer was small. The two sons of Rabi'ah, Utbah and Shaybah, owned that garden, and seeing him against their wall they sent out a Christian servant with a tray of grapes. He said Bismillah before eating and the servant stopped: people in this land do not say that. Where are you from, the Prophet ﷺ asked, and what is your religion. I am a Christian, he said, from Nineveh. Then you are from the town of the righteous Yunus son of Matta. Addas asked what he could possibly know of Yunus. He said: he is my brother; he was a prophet and so am I. Addas bent and kissed his head, his hands and his feet. His owners watched, and told him afterwards that his own religion was better than that man's.

The second answer came further along the road, and Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim both carry it, from Urwah, from Aishah — who had asked him whether he had ever known a day worse than Uhud. He answered that his people had troubled him a great deal, and the worst of it was the day he presented himself to Ibn Abd Yalil bin Abd Kulal and received no response. He left overwhelmed with sorrow and did not stop until he found himself at Qarn ath-Tha'alib, where he raised his head and saw a cloud shading him. Jibreel called from it: Allah has heard what your people said to you and the reply they gave you, and has sent you the angel of the mountains to order as you wish. The angel greeted him and offered to bring the two mountains down on the town.

He said no. I hope Allah will bring from them children who worship Allah alone and associate nothing with Him.

The revelation itself came at Wadi Nakhlah on the way home, and it was not about Ta'if at all. A company of jinn stood and listened to him reciting without his knowing they were there, and Allah sent it down to inform him: «قُلْ أُوحِيَ إِلَيَّ أَنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ نَفَرٌ مِّنَ الْجِنِّ» (72:1). The same night is described in 46:29-31, where the listeners go back to their own people as warners.

What it settled was not the grievance. It settled the standing of the message. He had spent ten days asking for a single hearing in Ta'if and been refused by every man in it. On the road out, a hearing was given from a direction he had not thought to ask, and beyond anyone's power to veto.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 72:1 — «قُلْ أُوحِيَ إِلَيَّ أَنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ نَفَرٌ مِّنَ الْجِنِّ» 'Say: it has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened'; see also 46:29-31
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — narrated by Aishah from Urwah, the angel of the mountains
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam — citing Ibn Hisham for the account of Addas

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: He came home under another man's spears
layers.content:
He could not simply walk back in. From near Makkah he sent a man of Khuza'ah to Al-Akhnas bin Shuraiq asking for protection; the answer was that he was an ally of Quraysh and in no position to give it. He sent to Suhail bin Amr; also nothing. Then Al-Mut'im bin Adi — one of the five who had broken the boycott — volunteered. He had his people arm themselves fully, walked the Prophet ﷺ into the Sacred Masjid, waited while he prayed two rak'ah, and escorted him to his own door.

Abu Jahl asked Al-Mut'im afterwards whether that was protection or conversion. Protection, he said. Abu Jahl was satisfied, and said that for Mut'im's sake he would extend it too. Years later at Badr, standing over seventy prisoners, the Prophet ﷺ said that if Mut'im bin Adi were alive and had asked him for these rotten people, he would have handed them over. Sahih al-Bukhari carries that.

In Shawwal of the same year he married Sawdah bint Zam'ah, a widow of the emigration to Abyssinia, the first he married after Khadijah.

And he named the year. The rapid succession of losses led him to call it the Year of Grief and Sorrow, and the name stuck to it permanently.

Here is the thing to carry. He did not name it a year of victory in disguise. He named it what it was, and the sirah kept the name. Grief was not treated as a failure of faith to be argued away — it was recorded, dated and titled. Then notice what he actually did inside it: he complained upward and not outward, refused an offer to destroy the town that had bled him, and hoped out loud for the children of his tormentors. In the worst year of his life, when he was handed real power over the people who had hurt him, he did not use it. Ta'if would come into Islam within a decade, and its people would be the descendants he had asked for.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the Prophet ﷺ on Al-Mut'im bin Adi after Badr
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam — citing Ibn Hisham and Ibn Al-Qayyim, Zad Al-Ma'ad

quiz.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ say when Abu Talib finally refused to say the word of testimony?

options.text: He said nothing and left the room
By Allah, I will keep asking pardon for you until I am forbidden to do so
He declared that his uncle's protection had been repaid in full
He asked Abu Jahl and Abdullah bin Abi Umaiyah to leave the house

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari — narrated from al-Musayyab; Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Two men sat at that bedside asking Abu Talib to hold on to the religion of his father. The sirah records that they got their answer.

quiz.prompt: Who travelled with the Prophet ﷺ on foot to Ta'if?

options.text: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
Ali ibn Abi Talib
Zayd bin Harithah
Al-Abbas bin Abdul-Muttalib

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: Sixty kilometres out and sixty back, on foot. Zayd took a head wound trying to shield him from the stones on the way out of the town.

quiz.prompt: The angel of the mountains offered to bring the two mountains down on the people of Ta'if. What did the Prophet ﷺ answer?

options.text: He accepted, and the punishment was later withheld
He asked for a delay of one year
No — I hope Allah will bring from them children who worship Allah alone
He left the decision to Jibreel

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — narrated by Aishah from Urwah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was still bleeding from their stones when the offer was made. He asked for their grandchildren instead.

options.text: A chief of Thaqif who accepted Islam in secret
A Christian servant of the sons of Rabi'ah, from Nineveh
A Jewish scholar of Ta'if who recognised the description
A merchant of Khuza'ah who carried the message to Makkah

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was sent out with a tray of grapes and no expectation of anything. He came back having kissed the head, hands and feet of the man his owners were mocking.

quiz.prompt: What was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ at Wadi Nakhlah on the journey back from Ta'if?

options.text: The verses of Surah Al-Qamar about the splitting of the moon
That a company of jinn had listened to his recitation — Surah Al-Jinn, and 46:29-31
The command to migrate to Madinah
The prohibition on asking forgiveness for the idolaters

quiz.citation: Quran 72:1-15 and 46:29-31 — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Al-Mubarakpuri notes from the wording of the verses that he did not know they were there. He was informed of his own audience by revelation.

quiz.prompt: The supplication at the wall begins by complaining of his own weakness and his own lowliness before people. What is that?

options.text: An honest description of his position, offered without any decoration
The opposite of complaint — a complaint made only to Allah stops being one
Permission for every believer to bring Allah the actual state they are in
A refusal to accuse anyone but himself, even when others had just stoned him

quiz.slider_label: How honest are you with Allah about how badly it is going?
quiz.citation: The supplication at Ta'if — reported by Ibn Ishaq, carried in Ibn Hisham and in Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar; not in Bukhari or Muslim
quiz.scholar_reflection: He does not ask for revenge, rescue, or an easier assignment. He states his weakness and asks whose hands he is being placed in.

quiz.prompt: Abu Talib shielded the call for a decade and died refusing the word. How do you hold both halves of that?

options.text: Loyalty and belief are separate things, and he had one without the other
The good a person does is real even when it does not save them
It shows that nobody is carried into faith by proximity, not even the man in the next room
It is simply painful, and the sirah does not resolve it for us

quiz.slider_label: How much can one person's faith do for another?
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari — the deathbed of Abu Talib; and the hadith of Al-Abbas bin Abdul-Muttalib
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ was asked whether his uncle's protection had availed him. He answered that Mut'im's kind of loyalty lightened a punishment; it did not remove it.

quiz.prompt: A whole city refused him over ten days, and one foreign slave in a garden believed him in a few minutes. What does that arrangement say?

options.text: Guidance does not follow status, wealth, or the order you would predict
One person hearing you is not a small result — it is the whole result
The nobles had too much to lose; the slave had nothing to protect
Allah answered a supplication with a person, not with a rescue

quiz.slider_label: Would you count one person as enough?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham — the account of Addas
quiz.scholar_reflection: The two men who sent the grapes stayed disbelievers and died at Badr. Their servant recognised prophethood from one sentence about Yunus.

quiz.prompt: He was handed real, immediate power over the town that had just bled him — and declined it. Why do you think he declined?

options.text: Because the mission was never about winning the argument with Ta'if
Because he was thinking about generations he would never meet
Because mercy is not a mood he happened to be in; it was the assignment
Because destroying them would have ended the possibility of ever guiding them

quiz.slider_label: What would you have done with that offer?
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — narrated by Aishah from Urwah
quiz.scholar_reflection: Within about ten years, Thaqif came to Madinah and accepted Islam. The children he asked for are on the record.

quiz.prompt: He called that year the Year of Grief and Sorrow, and the name was kept. What do you take from him naming it that?

options.text: That grief is not a defect in faith to be explained away
That the Prophet ﷺ was permitted his own sorrow, and so are we
That naming a hard thing accurately is part of surviving it
That he mourned openly and still went to Ta'if the same season

quiz.slider_label: How do you name your own worst year?
quiz.scholar_reflection: Of Khadijah he said she believed him when the people disbelieved him. He was still saying it years after her death, in Madinah, with other wives in the house.
